questions.label: Problem 1
questions.statement: Design a Turing machine that adds one in tally notation. The tape starts with a single block of strokes representing x, with the head on the rightmost stroke. The machine must halt leaving a single block of x + 1 strokes, with the head back on the rightmost stroke of the block.

questions.label: Problem 2
questions.statement: Design a Turing machine that computes x + 3 in tally notation, reusing your solution to the add-one problem. The tape starts with a single block of strokes representing x, with the head on the rightmost stroke, and the machine must halt leaving a single block of x + 3 strokes in standard position.

questions.label: Problem 3
questions.statement: Design a Turing machine that multiplies its input by three in tally notation, building on your solution to the x + 3 problem. The tape starts with a single block of strokes representing x, with the head on the rightmost stroke, and the machine must halt leaving a single block of 3x strokes in standard position.

questions.label: Problem 4
questions.statement: Design a Turing machine that adds two numbers in tally notation. The tape starts with two blocks of strokes: the block for y on the left and the block for x on the right, with the head on the rightmost stroke of the x block. The machine must halt leaving a single block of x + y strokes in standard position. Do not assume the two blocks are separated by exactly one empty cell; a robust machine should work when they are separated by any number of empty cells.

questions.label: Problem 5
questions.statement: Design a Turing machine that computes three times the sum of its two inputs in tally notation, reusing your addition and tripling constructions. The tape starts with the y block on the left and the x block on the right, with the head on the rightmost stroke of the x block, and the machine must halt leaving a single block of 3(x + y) strokes in standard position.

questions.label: Problem 6
questions.statement: Design a Turing machine that computes x + 3y in tally notation, reusing your earlier constructions. The tape starts with the y block on the left and the x block on the right, with the head on the rightmost stroke of the x block, and the machine must halt leaving a single block of x + 3y strokes in standard position.

questions.label: Problem 7
questions.statement: Design a Turing machine that adds one to a binary numeral. The tape starts with the numeral of x written between two asterisk markers, with the head on the right marker, and the machine must halt leaving one well-formed block containing the binary numeral of x + 1, with the head back on the block's right marker.

questions.label: Problem 8
questions.statement: Design a Turing machine that subtracts one from a binary numeral, outputting zero when the input is zero. The tape starts with the numeral of x written between two asterisk markers, with the head on the right marker. The machine must halt leaving one well-formed block containing the binary numeral of x - 1 when x is at least one, and the numeral 0 when x is zero, ending with the head on the block's right marker.
questions.notes: Bank hand-authored: f(x) = max(0, x - 1) is inexpressible in the authoring DSL (negative intermediate on x = 0), so the standard 16-value binary TM sample is mapped through the floor directly; cc_spec intentionally omitted (the tape axis grades from representation + test_cases alone).

questions.label: Problem 9
questions.statement: Design a Turing machine that adds two binary numerals, reusing your add-one and subtract-one machines. The tape starts with the numeral of y between asterisk markers on the left and the numeral of x between asterisk markers on the right, with the head on the rightmost marker. The machine must transfer the value of x into the y block one unit at a time, then erase everything except a single well-formed block containing the binary numeral of x + y — clean up so that exactly one pair of markers remains on the tape.

questions.label: Problem 10
questions.statement: Multiplication: x • y. Using a combination of flow charts, prose, and "snapshots" of the tape, describe a step-by-step strategy for computing multiplication. This should not be a complete Turing Machine. (That is a difficult and laborious problem.) But it should be sufficiently detailed that you think someone could build a Turing Machine from your instructions, if they knew what they were doing. Your choice of Tally or Binary.

questions.label: Problem 11
questions.statement: Multi-function machine. Design a machine which can perform different functions depending on the user input (at least successor, addition, multiplication), similar to a calculator. There are many ways to do this, so be creative. Use a combination of flow charts, prose, and "snapshots" of the tape; don’t design a completed Turing Machine.
